name: Sauna

angle.text: Looksmaxxers use sauna to debloat the face, aid recovery and gains, and, in some claims, increase brow-ridge bone mass. Cardiovascular research from Finnish cohorts is substantial; the facial and bone claims have no studies.

summary: Heat bathing with a strong cardiovascular research base in Finnish cohorts, and no studies at all on the facial and bone claims made online.
note: Evidence for appearance outcomes (debloating, hormones, bone) is absent; alcohol, dehydration and some heart conditions raise risk.
currentQuick:
A sauna is a heated room, traditionally Finnish, held at roughly 70-105 C with low humidity, in which people sit to sweat. In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a way to reduce facial puffiness, aid recovery and sleep, and supposedly raise growth hormone.
Published research is mostly about heart and circulation health, largely from observational Finnish cohorts and small trials of heat therapy. Studies of facial appearance have not been published.
How it works: Heat exposure causes sweating, vasodilation and raised heart rate, a mild cardiovascular load resembling light exercise. Researchers link repeated exposure to improved endothelial function and lower blood pressure; claims about bone or facial structure have no mechanism supported by published studies.
Risks and caveats: Medical reviews report that alcohol, dehydration and certain heart conditions (such as unstable angina or severe aortic stenosis) increase risk, and that pregnancy calls for limits on core temperature. Rapid sweat-based weight loss is a studied practice in combat sports with documented physiological effects.
deepLead:
A sauna is a small room heated to high temperatures, typically 70-105 C with low humidity, where people sit to sweat, often with bursts of steam made by pouring water on hot stones.  The practice is most associated with Finland, whose sauna culture UNESCO listed as intangible cultural heritage in 2020.  Variants include smoke, electric, steam and infrared saunas. 
In looksmaxxing and wider wellness communities, sauna use is discussed for reducing water-retention puffiness, post-training recovery, sleep, and claimed hormonal effects.  Forum users also circulate a purported study claiming large increases in brow-ridge bone mass; no such study appears in the published literature.
Published research centres on cardiovascular outcomes. A Finnish prospective cohort found that more frequent sauna bathing was associated with lower rates of sudden cardiac death, fatal cardiovascular disease and all-cause mortality.  Small trials of repeated heat exposure report improved vascular function.  No clinical studies have examined sauna use for facial appearance.

name: Magnesium oil / Epsom salt bath

angle.text: Users soak in Epsom salt or spray magnesium chloride brine on the skin for muscle relaxation and better sleep, tied to recovery and a rested look. Transdermal magnesium claims have little published trial support.

summary: Soaking in magnesium sulfate or applying magnesium chloride brine, popular for transdermal magnesium claims that have little published trial support.
note: Sources reviewed contain no trials of skin absorption or appearance effects.
currentQuick:
Epsom salt is magnesium sulfate, long sold as bath salts for sore muscles and feet. Magnesium oil is a concentrated magnesium chloride brine applied to skin. Online, both are promoted as ways to raise magnesium levels through the skin, for sleep, recovery and relaxation.
The sources reviewed for this entry do not include trials of absorption through skin or of any appearance outcome.
How it works: Proponents propose that magnesium passes through the skin during a soak or topical application. Encyclopedic sources describe bath use for soothing sore feet and its role in bath salts, without stating that skin absorption occurs.
Risks and caveats: Magnesium sulfate is given internally in medicine for deficiency and other conditions, where dosing is clinical. Epsom salt in baths is widely sold over the counter; no safety data from the sources reviewed address bath use specifically.
deepLead:
Epsom salt is the common name for magnesium sulfate heptahydrate, named after a saline spring in Epsom, Surrey, England.  It is used externally as bath salts, especially foot soaks to soothe sore feet.  Magnesium oil, despite its name, is typically a magnesium chloride brine sprayed on skin; it is a separate product.
In looksmaxxing and wellness circles, both are promoted for transdermal magnesium delivery, aimed at sleep, muscle recovery and relaxation. Medical uses of magnesium sulfate are internal, such as replacing magnesium in deficiency and treating certain conditions in hospital.

name: Grounding / earthing mat

angle.text: Users sleep on conductive sheets and mats connected to the earth, believing it improves sleep and wellbeing and so a more rested appearance. Published evidence for sleep or appearance benefits is limited.

summary: Conductive sheets and mats meant to connect the sleeper to the earth, with no strong published evidence for sleep or appearance benefits in the sources reviewed.
note: Sources reviewed contain no trials; it is classed as an alternative medicine practice.
currentQuick:
Grounding or earthing products are conductive mats, sheets or bands that plug into a wall socket's ground port or a ground rod. Marketing and community posts say sleeping connected to the earth improves sleep and reduces inflammation.
Encyclopedic sources list earthing as an alternative medicine practice. No trials were retrieved for this entry.
How it works: Proponents claim that electrons from the earth's surface neutralise free radicals in the body. The sources reviewed give no published mechanistic evidence supporting this.
Risks and caveats: The product is a passive conductive fabric, but connection through a wall outlet raises electrical-safety questions that manufacturers address with built-in resistors; sources reviewed provide no safety data.
deepLead:
Grounding or earthing refers to an alternative medicine practice in which people make direct contact with the earth, or with conductive products connected to it, in the belief that this improves health.  Grounding mats and sheets are sold for sleep and plug into a socket's ground port.
Wikipedia lists earthing under energy medicine and as an alternative medicine practice.  No clinical studies were retrieved for this entry, and the looksmaxxing-specific claim of improved sleep and appearance is not documented in the sources reviewed.

name: Mouth breathing correction / myofunctional therapy

angle.text: Users practice nasal breathing, tongue and lip exercises, and lip taping, to improve breathing and, they believe, jaw and facial structure. Myofunctional therapy is studied for breathing; the facial claims rest mostly on conceptual models.

summary: Tongue, lip and nasal-breathing exercises promoted to improve breathing and facial structure, with the facial claims resting mostly on conceptual models.
note: Evidence for changing adult facial structure was not found in the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
Mouth breathing correction covers exercises and habits meant to encourage nasal breathing and proper tongue posture, sometimes with lip taping at night. Communities link it to jaw development, facial shape and sleep apnea.
Encyclopedic sources say chronic mouth breathing in children may affect facial growth, but support comes mainly from textbooks, reviews and conceptual models.
How it works: Proponents say tongue posture and nasal airflow shape the jaws and airway. Sources describe mouth breathing as most often a response to nasal congestion, with treatment aimed at the underlying cause and building a nasal breathing habit.
Risks and caveats: The health effects of mouth taping have been little researched, according to encyclopedic sources. Persistent mouth breathing can reflect nasal obstruction that merits assessment.
deepLead:
Mouth breathing correction describes efforts to shift breathing from the mouth to the nose, including exercises of the tongue and lips known as myofunctional therapy and, in some communities, taping the lips shut during sleep. 
In about 85% of cases, mouth breathing is described as an adaptation to nasal congestion.  Chronic mouth breathing in children has been proposed to influence dental and facial growth, including a long, narrow face, though the relationship may run in both directions. 
Support for these links comes mainly from textbooks, reviews and conceptual models, and the health effects of mouth taping are little researched.

name: CPAP (sleep apnea)

angle.text: CPAP is the standard treatment for moderate to severe sleep apnea, and online discussion links the better sleep with less facial puffiness and a fresher appearance. Appearance benefits are untested in the sources reviewed.

summary: The standard treatment for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea; appearance benefits like less puffiness are discussed online but untested in the sources reviewed.
note: Prescription medical device; appearance outcomes not studied in the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
CPAP delivers air at constant pressure through a mask to keep the airway open during sleep. It is described as the most effective treatment for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea.
In looksmaxxing communities it is discussed as a way to improve puffiness and facial appearance by treating apnea. The sources reviewed do not test appearance outcomes.
How it works: Pressurised air splints the upper airway open, eliminating obstructive apneas in most people who use it as directed. Nasal, full-face, and hybrid masks exist.
Risks and caveats: Adherence is a major problem: about 8% stop after the first night and more than half within a year. Reported side effects include discomfort, congestion, bloating, claustrophobia and mask leaks.
deepLead:
Continuous positive airway pressure (CPAP) delivers pressurised air through a mask to keep the airway open during sleep.  It was developed in adults by Colin Sullivan, who built a machine in 1980 at Royal Prince Alfred Hospital in Sydney, and Respironics began selling a commercial adult device in 1985. 
It is described as the most effective treatment for moderate to severe obstructive sleep apnea and, in people with sleep apnea, lowers overall risk of cardiovascular death.  Case series have reported reduced seizure frequency in people with epilepsy and sleep apnea who used CPAP. 
Looksmaxxing communities discuss CPAP for facial puffiness and appearance; no appearance studies were found.

name: Sleep apnea surgery / MMA

angle.text: Maxillomandibular advancement moves the upper and lower jaws forward to open the airway, and it is discussed in looksmaxxing circles for the visible change to the facial profile. The skeletal change is plainly measurable; it is described as among the most effective sleep surgeries.

summary: Maxillomandibular advancement moves both jaws forward to open the airway, described as among the most effective sleep surgeries and often discussed for facial change.
note: Major surgery with longer recovery than other sleep procedures; appearance outcomes not covered by the sources reviewed.
currentQuick:
Maxillomandibular advancement (MMA) surgically moves the upper and lower jaws forward, enlarging the airway behind the tongue. It is described as one of the most effective surgical treatments for sleep apnea.
Communities discuss it for apnea and for its effects on jaw projection. The sources reviewed do not describe appearance outcomes.
How it works: Advancing the jaws pulls attached tissues forward, widening the airway. It is often paired with genioglossus advancement and usually considered after other treatments such as nasal surgery or tonsillectomy have failed.
Risks and caveats: Recovery is longer than for other sleep apnea surgeries because the facial bones must heal in their new position. Risk details were not provided in the sources reviewed.
deepLead:
Maxillomandibular advancement (MMA), also called bimaxillary advancement or orthognathic surgery, moves the upper and lower jaws forward.  It was first used to correct facial skeletal deformities and malocclusion, and from the late 1970s advancing the lower jaw was noted to improve sleepiness in patients. 
It is described as one of the most effective surgical treatments for obstructive sleep apnea, often done with genioglossus advancement and usually after other treatments fail.  Recovery is longer than for other sleep surgeries. 
Registered trials are ongoing or planned, including comparisons of splintless versus conventional MMA.

name: Face tape / sleep patches for wrinkles

angle.text: Users stick tape or silicone patches on the forehead, brows and eyes before bed to smooth lines and prevent new ones forming. They are sold as cosmetic products with strong marketing; trial data on wrinkles is absent.

summary: Overnight forehead and brow stickers promising to smooth lines in your sleep, with marketing behind them and no trial data.
note: No published trials; adhesives can irritate skin.
currentQuick:
Face tape and sleep patches are stickers worn overnight on areas that crease, such as the forehead, brow or around the eyes. They are marketed as preventing or softening expression and sleep lines.
No clinical studies of them for wrinkles were found. Established wrinkle treatments are different products entirely, such as botulinum toxin and prescription retinoids.
How it works: The idea is that holding skin flat and occluded overnight reduces creasing from movement and pillow pressure. Occlusion is known to reduce water loss from skin, but an effect on permanent wrinkles has not been tested.
Risks and caveats: Adhesives can cause irritation or contact dermatitis in some people. They are sold as cosmetics without a wrinkle-treatment approval.
deepLead:
Face tape and sleep patches are adhesive strips or silicone and hydrocolloid-style pads that people stick on the forehead, between the brows, around the eyes or on the mouth area before bed, with the aim of flattening or preventing lines that form from facial expression or sleeping position. They are sold as cosmetic products and are not medical devices with a recognised wrinkle indication.
Wrinkles are generally attributed to a mix of repeated facial movement, ageing, sun exposure, smoking, low hydration and habitual sleeping position. Treatments with an established evidence base are different in kind: botulinum toxin, which is FDA-approved for glabellar (frown) lines, and the prescription retinoids tretinoin and tazarotene. Wikipedia's wrinkle article does not mention tape or patches.
No published clinical trials of face tape or sleep patches for wrinkles were located in the sources reviewed for this article. Claims about them rest mainly on manufacturer marketing and user testimonials.

name: Overnight skin repair routine (retinol at night)

angle.text: Skincare communities apply retinol with a moisturiser in the evening to address fine lines, texture and sun damage. Retinoids have real wrinkle evidence; the overnight timing framing has not been tested separately.

summary: Retinol at bedtime with a moisturiser; retinoids have real wrinkle evidence, but the 'overnight' framing itself hasn't been tested.
note: Irritation common; retinoids avoided in pregnancy.
currentQuick:
This routine means using retinol, a vitamin A derivative, in the evening, usually followed by a moisturiser. It is aimed at fine lines, roughness and sun-damaged skin.
Retinoids as a class have supporting evidence for photoaging, strongest for prescription tretinoin. Retinol is weaker but has some support, and effects fade after stopping.
How it works: Retinol converts in skin to retinoic acid, which stimulates collagen and slows its breakdown. Evening use is linked to retinol's light instability and reported sun sensitivity.
Risks and caveats: Redness, dryness and flaking are common. Retinoids are generally avoided in pregnancy, and the EU and UK capped retinol concentrations in 2025.
deepLead:
An overnight skin repair routine is a practice of applying retinol, often alongside a moisturiser or barrier-supporting product, in the evening so that the skin is treated while the person sleeps. It is common in skincare communities and appearance-focused circles as a way to address fine lines, texture and sun damage.
Retinol is the alcohol form of vitamin A and is converted in the skin to retinoic acid, the active form. It has been sold over the counter in cosmetics since 1984. Clinical and histological improvement in fine wrinkles has been reported, but benefits are not maintained after use stops. The better-studied retinoid is prescription tretinoin, which has trials up to two years in photoaging.
Reasons given for night-time use include that retinol is chemically unstable and sensitive to light and oxygen, and that retinoid-treated skin may become more sun-sensitive.

name: Overnight lip/eye masks

angle.text: Users apply thick lip and eye masks before bed to wake up with softer, less dry lips and a smoother look around the eyes. The moisturising effect is visible by morning; the masks themselves have not been trialled.

summary: Thick balms and gels left on overnight for lips and eyes; plain moisturiser logic, no trials of the masks themselves.
currentQuick:
These are rich moisturising products worn overnight on the lips or around the eyes. People use them to wake up with less dryness.
The general principle of occlusive moisturisers is documented, but no studies of the branded masks were found.
How it works: Occlusive ingredients trap moisture by slowing water loss, while humectants attract water. Effects are on hydration, not structure.
Risks and caveats: Irritation or allergic contact dermatitis from fragrance or other ingredients is possible. Paraffin-based products are flammable.
deepLead:
Overnight lip and eye masks are leave-on products, usually a thick balm, gel or sheet, applied before bed and left on while sleeping. They are marketed to moisturise the lips and the thin skin around the eyes and to soften the look of dryness and fine lines by morning.
Most work on general moisturiser principles: occlusives such as petrolatum form a film that slows water loss, and humectants attract water. Sleep masks that cover the eyes are a separate product, used to block light. No clinical trial of these specific overnight masks was located.

name: Polyphasic sleep

angle.text: Online communities try schedules such as Uberman and Everyman to cut total sleep to a few hours, freeing time for training and other pursuits. Expert panels report adverse impacts, and the claim that short naps replace most night sleep is unproven.

summary: Splitting sleep into naps to sleep far less; historically interesting, and expert panels report adverse impacts.
note: Chronic sleep restriction risk; NSF panel reports adverse impact.
currentQuick:
Polyphasic sleep means sleeping in several short blocks per day instead of one long night. Online schedules like Uberman try to cut total sleep to two to four hours.
Biphasic or segmented sleep has a documented history, but evidence that extreme reduction works is absent, and a 2021 expert panel reported adverse effects.
How it works: Followers time short naps to catch REM or deep sleep early, relying on adaptation. Evidence for this is limited to small, short studies.
Risks and caveats: Sleep restriction, circadian disruption and microsleeps are the main risks reported by sleep organisations.
deepLead:
Polyphasic sleep is the practice of dividing sleep into several separate periods across 24 hours, usually more than two, rather than one consolidated nighttime block. The term was used in the early twentieth century by psychologist J. S. Szymanski to describe animal activity patterns. In online communities it refers to schedules, such as Uberman and Everyman, that aim to cut total sleep to a few hours using short naps.
Historical research suggests segmented nighttime sleep was common in pre-industrial Europe, a view argued by historian A. Roger Ekirch in 2001, though a 2015 study of three pre-industrial societies found monophasic nighttime sleep and Ekirch has questioned its conclusions. Wikipedia states there is no scientific evidence that extreme reduced-sleep schedules are effective or beneficial. A 2021 National Sleep Foundation consensus panel report addressed the adverse impact of polyphasic sleep patterns in humans.

name: Napping / NSDR / yoga nidra

angle.text: Users nap or do NSDR and yoga nidra to make up for lost sleep and lower stress, aiming for a rested, less drawn look. Naps have been studied for alertness and performance; yoga nidra has small studies on relaxation, and none look at appearance.

summary: Short naps and guided deep-rest sessions for recovery; naps have decent evidence, yoga nidra is promising but small.
note: Long habitual naps associated with health risks in observational data.
currentQuick:
These are brief rest practices: daytime naps, and guided relaxation known as yoga nidra or NSDR.
Naps show benefits for alertness and learning, while yoga nidra research is small.
How it works: Naps restore alertness through short sleep; yoga nidra uses guided body awareness to produce deep relaxation.
Risks and caveats: Long naps can cause grogginess, and habitual long napping is linked observationally with health risks.
deepLead:
Napping, non-sleep deep rest (NSDR) and yoga nidra are short rest practices used to recover energy or reduce stress. A nap is a short daytime sleep period; yoga nidra is a guided meditation done lying down, often described as between waking and sleeping. NSDR is a more recent label popularised for similar guided-rest protocols; it is not mentioned in Wikipedia's yoga nidra article.
Evidence for naps is moderate for alertness and memory; evidence for yoga nidra is described as promising but limited.

name: Deload weeks / rest days

angle.text: Lifters schedule deloads and rest days so fatigue dissipates and training can continue progressing toward a more muscular physique. The approach rests on periodization theory; direct trials of deloads are sparse and none measure appearance.

summary: Planned lighter training weeks and rest days; grounded in periodization theory, little direct deload data.
currentQuick:
A deload is a planned lighter week of training; rest days are days off. Lifters use them to manage fatigue.
Periodization has a long theoretical history, but deloads as such have little direct research.
How it works: The idea is that reducing load allows fatigue to dissipate while fitness is retained.
Risks and caveats: Overtraining, from insufficient recovery, is the documented concern; deloads themselves carry no specific reported harms.
deepLead:
Deload weeks and rest days are planned reductions in training load, used by lifters and athletes to manage fatigue and recover. A deload is typically a week of reduced volume or intensity; rest days are days without training.
The concept relates to periodization, a cyclical method for planning training rooted in Hans Selye's general adaptation syndrome and formalised by Leo Matveyev around 1964. Wikipedia's periodization article does not use the word 'deload' but describes transition phases of 3-4 weeks and alternating hard and light days. Overtraining, a failure to recover, is typically treated with rest and reduced load.

name: Massage / foam rolling / recovery gear

angle.text: Foam rollers and massage tools are used to ease soreness and loosen tight muscles so users can train more often and move better, with a view to physique and posture. Studies report some short-term mobility and soreness benefits; appearance outcomes are not studied.

summary: Foam rollers and massage tools for muscle recovery: some short-term mobility benefit in studies, little appearance-specific evidence.
note: Research supports short-term range-of-motion changes; evidence for recovery is mixed.
currentQuick:
Foam rolling means rolling a muscle over a foam cylinder using body weight. People use it to feel less sore and more flexible.
It is discussed under posture and recovery rather than as a direct appearance tool.
How it works: Body weight presses the muscle against the roller, a form of self-myofascial release. Researchers have reported short-term increases in joint range of motion; long-term effects are unknown.[1]
Risks and caveats: The sources reviewed do not describe specific risks. Reviews describe the evidence as favouring use as a warm-up rather than as a recovery tool.
deepLead:
Foam rollers are lightweight cylinders of elastomeric foam that a person places between a muscle and the floor and rolls over using body weight, a practice classed as self-myofascial release. Proponents use them, along with related massage tools, to increase flexibility, reduce soreness and ease muscle knots.
In posture and body-recovery discussions, such tools are grouped as recovery gear. Published research summarized on Wikipedia reports a short-term improvement in joint range of motion, unknown long-term effects, and a view that the evidence better supports foam rolling as a warm-up activity than as a recovery tool, although post-exercise rolling has been reported to reduce perceived muscle pain.

name: Creatine for sleep deprivation

chain: Less cognitive hit from poor sleep
angle.text: Fitness and looksmaxxing posters take creatine to cushion the mental slump after short nights, so training and routines stay on track for physique goals. Small studies have examined cognition under sleep loss; none address how sleep-deprived people look.

summary: Creatine taken to blunt the cognitive hit of lost sleep: small studies exist, nothing on looks.
note: Evidence concerns cognition, not appearance; reviews are mixed.
currentQuick:
Creatine is a common muscle supplement. Some claim it helps the brain cope with sleep deprivation.
A few small experiments have tested this on cognitive tests; none tested appearance.
How it works: Creatine helps regenerate ATP in muscle and brain, and researchers have proposed it may support brain energy metabolism under stress.[1][3]
Risks and caveats: At standard doses reviews report mainly water-retention weight gain and stomach upset, with no kidney damage in healthy people; data are lacking for children and pregnancy.[1]
deepLead:
Creatine is an organic compound that helps regenerate ATP in muscle and brain tissue and is widely sold as a dietary supplement. Some people in fitness and looksmaxxing circles claim it can offset the cognitive effects of lost sleep.
Small experimental studies have examined this. A 2007 study tested creatine supplementation alongside sleep deprivation and exercise on cognition, mood and hormones, and a 2026 study reported that a single dose reduced sleep-deprivation-related deterioration in cognitive performance. Reviews of creatine and cognition more broadly report mixed results and an EFSA opinion that a cause-and-effect link cannot be established. None of this concerns facial appearance.

name: Sleep banking

angle.text: People sleep extra ahead of a planned short-sleep stretch, such as travel or a heavy schedule, hoping to stay sharp and look rested. It has been studied in military and shift-work settings with unsettled results, and not for appearance.

summary: Sleeping extra ahead of planned sleep loss: studied in military and shift-work settings, with unsettled evidence.
note: Researchers still debate whether a sleep surplus can be stored.
currentQuick:
Sleep banking means sleeping extra before an expected stretch of poor sleep.
Military and shift-work researchers study it, and recent reviews describe the evidence as still developing.
How it works: Believers say extra sleep builds a reserve that cushions later impairment; researchers are debating whether sleep-dependent brain resources can be stored.[1][2]
Risks and caveats: No specific harms are described in the sources reviewed. Sleep guidance cited recommends at least seven hours nightly for adults.[8]
deepLead:
Sleep banking, also called sleep extension, is the practice of sleeping more than usual in the days before an expected period of sleep loss, in the hope of reducing later impairment. It is discussed in military, shift-work and medical contexts and in some self-improvement circles.
Research is limited. A 2025 commentary in the journal Sleep debated whether banking produces a surplus of sleep-dependent brain resources, and a 2026 narrative review examined its role in reducing cognitive and motor impairment from later sleep restriction. Sleep medicine bodies cited on Wikipedia say the only sure way to counter sleep deprivation is more nightly sleep.

name: Sleep to look attractive (beauty sleep research)

angle.text: Appearance communities treat enough sleep as a baseline for a fresher face, citing research in which sleep-deprived faces were rated as less healthy and less attractive. Visible signs of sleep loss such as puffy eyes, paler skin and droopy lids are documented in studies.

summary: The belief that enough sleep makes you look better: visible signs of sleep loss are documented.
currentQuick:
Beauty sleep is the idea that sleep affects how attractive you look.
Documented effects of sleep loss include eye bags and puffiness.
How it works: People simply sleep enough; sleep loss is associated with visible signs around the eyes.[1]
Risks and caveats: Sleep loss is linked to cognitive, mood and health effects; no risks of sleeping adequately are described.
deepLead:
The idea of beauty sleep holds that adequate sleep improves how a person looks and that sleep-deprived faces are judged less attractive. It is a staple of appearance advice and looksmaxxing discussion.
Sleep medicine sources note that sleep deprivation produces visible signs including eye bags, periorbital puffiness and styes, and that extreme sleepiness made people feel about 10 years older in one study. This article was written from limited sources; studies that directly measured attractiveness ratings were not available to cite.

name: Eight hours target / 'sleep is looksmaxxing'

angle.text: 'Sleep is looksmaxxing' is a community slogan treating regular sleep, often about eight hours, as the foundation for skin, recovery and body composition. Adult sleep guidance recommends 7 to 9 hours, and sleep loss has documented visible effects on the face.

summary: Sleep as the baseline looksmax: eight hours is a community target, guidance says 7 to 9 for adults.
currentQuick:
This is the belief that sleep comes first among looksmaxxing habits, usually with an eight-hour goal.
Public guidance recommends roughly 7 to 9 hours for adults.
How it works: Proponents say adequate sleep avoids visible signs such as eye bags.[1]
Risks and caveats: Habitual short sleep is associated with chronic health conditions.[1]
deepLead:
The phrase 'sleep is looksmaxxing' expresses the view in appearance communities that adequate sleep is the most basic appearance improvement, often with a target of about eight hours a night.
Guidance cited on Wikipedia varies: the US National Sleep Foundation recommends about 7 hours for adults, with other cited ranges of 7 to 9 hours for ages 18 to 64. Sleep deprivation is associated with eye bags, puffiness, weight gain and other effects.

name: Keto / ketogenic diet

angle.text: Some users follow keto to lean out and, in anecdotal accounts, to calm acne. It is established as a therapy for epilepsy, has mixed results for weight loss, and has not been tested for skin in the sources here.

summary: Very low-carb eating for leanness and acne claims: proven for epilepsy, mixed for weight, untested for skin here.
note: Case reports of ketoacidosis; raised lipids reported.
currentQuick:
Keto is a very low-carb, high-fat diet made for epilepsy.
People also use it to lose weight; some claim it clears acne.
How it works: With little carbohydrate, the liver makes ketone bodies that replace glucose as fuel.[1]
Risks and caveats: Reported effects include constipation, early fatigue, raised lipids, and rare ketoacidosis.[1][2]
deepLead:
The ketogenic diet is a high-fat, adequate-protein, very low-carbohydrate diet in which the liver produces ketone bodies as fuel. It was developed as a medical therapy for refractory epilepsy, mainly in children. Popularly it is used for weight loss, and some in looksmaxxing communities also use it for leaning out and for acne claims.
For weight loss, Wikipedia reports that low-carbohydrate diets produce somewhat more short-term loss than low-fat diets, with the advantage fading over time, and a 2022 Cochrane review found no benefit over balanced diets at two years. Acne effects are not covered in the sources consulted.

name: Low-carb diet

chain: Lower calorie intake, less water weight
angle.text: Users cut carbohydrates to lose fat and sharpen their physique, and some pair it with high protein to keep muscle while cutting. Trials show slightly faster early weight loss than low-fat diets, with the gap narrowing over time.

summary: Cutting carbs moderately: slightly faster early weight loss than low-fat diets in trials, with the gap fading over time, and a split of opinion on whether it suits the long term.
note: Definitions vary widely; very low-carb and ketogenic versions carry additional documented risks.
currentQuick:
A low-carb diet reduces bread, sugar, pasta and similar foods and replaces them with more protein and fat. There is no single agreed threshold: bodies and researchers variously define it as under 20 to 25 percent of calories from carbohydrate, with ketogenic versions going much lower.
In looksmaxxing circles it is discussed as a leanness and skin-clarity tool, and as the moderate alternative to carnivore diets. Some forum users report low energy, constant hunger and poor gym performance on it, while others tolerate it well.
How it works: Fewer carbohydrates means lower blood glucose swings and, at very low intakes, ketone production. Research suggests early weight loss is partly water and that longer-term results track calorie intake and adherence more than the macronutrient ratio. Higher protein intake may increase satiety.
Risks and caveats: Reported side effects include constipation, headache, bad breath, cramps and weakness. Long-term cohort data are mixed, and cardiology and dietetic bodies advise discussion with a clinician before very low-carb versions. Ketoacidosis is rare but documented, mostly in diabetes.
deepLead:
A low-carbohydrate diet restricts carbohydrate intake relative to typical Western eating, usually limiting sugars, bread, pasta and starches and relying more on meat, fish, eggs, dairy, nuts and non-starchy vegetables. There is no standard definition: one professional body treats under 20 percent of energy from carbohydrate as low-carb, another uses under 25 percent, and ketogenic variants typically go below about 50 grams a day. This makes studies difficult to compare.
In looksmaxxing communities the diet is discussed as a way to reduce body fat, improve skin and manage energy, and it is often positioned between ordinary eating and stricter carnivore regimens. Forum users hold opposing views, with some reporting that cutting carbohydrate left them hungry, fatigued and with poor training performance.
Published research generally finds that low-carb diets produce slightly more weight loss than low-fat diets in the short and medium term, with the difference small and diminishing over time; long-term outcomes appear to depend largely on calorie intake and adherence. Major health bodies differ in how they position the approach.

name: Beef, salt and water diet

angle.text: Followers of the lion diet eat only ruminant meat, salt and water, promoting it for leanness, clearer skin and mood. It rests on testimonials; no controlled studies of this diet exist.

summary: The most restrictive carnivore variant, popularised as the lion diet: ruminant meat, salt and water only, with no controlled evidence behind it.
note: Supported mainly by self-reports; dietitians' bodies classify carnivore diets as fad diets and flag nutrient gaps.
currentQuick:
This is a strict elimination-style version of the carnivore diet in which a person eats only beef or other ruminant meat, salt and water. It is often called the lion diet. It became widely known through Mikhaila Peterson and her father Jordan Peterson, who described following it.
Proponents describe it as a way to identify food sensitivities and to relieve autoimmune and mood symptoms. These accounts are anecdotal; no controlled trial has tested the diet.
How it works: Advocates say removing all plant foods and most other animal foods eliminates potential triggers such as plant compounds. Near-zero carbohydrate intake means the body relies on fat and protein for energy, usually in ketosis.
Risks and caveats: Critics cite missing fibre and micronutrients, raised LDL cholesterol, constipation and, with high red-meat intake, associations with colon cancer and gout. Grokipedia notes that early fatigue and cramps usually fade within weeks and that scurvy has been documented in a meat-only case.
deepLead:
The beef, salt and water diet is the strictest form of the carnivore diet, limiting intake to ruminant meat (mostly beef), salt and water. It is commonly called the lion diet.
Grokipedia reports that Mikhaila Peterson created the lion diet in 2017 as an elimination protocol for autoimmune arthritis and depression, and Wikipedia reports that she and her father Jordan Peterson publicly followed it, after which it became a viral social-media trend. Proponents rely largely on self-reports; the evidence base is described as very low quality, with no large randomised trials.
